clinicalPearls: In children an ACTH-secreting pituitary corticotroph adenoma is the commonest cause of endogenous Cushing syndrome beyond infancy
The hallmark is weight gain together with growth arrest, so a decelerating height velocity in a child who is gaining weight should prompt evaluation
Other features include facial rounding and plethora, striae, hypertension and fatigue, often more subtle than in adults
Delayed or arrested puberty and declining school performance may occur
The adenomas are usually small microadenomas that can be difficult to see on MRI

Diagnosis follows the standard hypercortisolism workup with late-night salivary or serum cortisol, 24-hour urinary free cortisol and low-dose dexamethasone suppression, then confirmation of ACTH dependence
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling is valuable to confirm a pituitary source and to lateralise when MRI is equivocal
First-line treatment is transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy, after which catch-up growth and recovery of the axis need monitoring
reference.pathophysiology: Paediatric Cushing disease is caused by a corticotroph adenoma of the anterior pituitary that autonomously secretes ACTH, driving bilateral adrenal cortisol overproduction. Chronic glucocorticoid excess suppresses the growth hormone and IGF-1 axis and directly inhibits growth-plate chondrocytes and bone formation, so linear growth slows or halts even as adiposity increases, giving the characteristic divergence of the height and weight curves in children. Cortisol excess also suppresses gonadotropin secretion and so delays puberty, raises blood pressure, impairs glucose tolerance and alters mood and immune function. The tumours are usually microadenomas, and the excess ACTH retains partial responsiveness to high-dose glucocorticoid feedback, which underlies the diagnostic testing.
additionalDifferentials: Exogenous (iatrogenic) glucocorticoid exposure, by far the commonest cause of a Cushingoid appearance
Simple exogenous obesity, where growth velocity is usually normal or increased
Ectopic ACTH secretion, which is rare in children
Adrenal adenoma or carcinoma causing ACTH-independent Cushing syndrome
Primary pigmented nodular adrenocortical disease and Carney complex
additionalInvestigations: Documentation of the growth curve and height velocity alongside weight
Late-night salivary or midnight serum cortisol to demonstrate loss of the diurnal rhythm
Plasma ACTH to establish ACTH dependence
Pituitary MRI, recognising that a microadenoma may be small or unseen
Inferior petrosal sinus sampling with CRH stimulation to confirm the pituitary source and lateralisation
redFlags: Progressive growth arrest with weight gain in a child
Very high cortisol or ACTH suggesting aggressive disease or an ectopic or adrenal malignancy
Vertebral fracture from osteoporosis, or significant psychiatric disturbance
reference.prognosis: Transsphenoidal surgery by an experienced neurosurgeon achieves remission in most children; catch-up growth is often incomplete so final height may be reduced, and there is a risk of persistent or recurrent disease requiring further surgery, radiotherapy or medical therapy, along with temporary secondary adrenal insufficiency during axis recovery.
pitfalls: Reassuring an obese child without checking the growth curve, since normal growth argues against Cushing disease and arrested growth is a red flag
Over-relying on a normal or equivocal MRI to exclude a microadenoma
Omitting inferior petrosal sinus sampling when imaging is negative but disease is ACTH-dependent
Failing to anticipate and treat postoperative adrenal insufficiency and to monitor for recurrence
references: Endocrine Society Clinical Practice Guideline on Cushing Syndrome
management: Transsphenoidal selective adenomectomy by an experienced pituitary neurosurgeon as first-line treatment
Pituitary radiotherapy, or medical steroidogenesis inhibitors such as metyrapone or ketoconazole, as second-line or bridging therapy
Postoperative glucocorticoid replacement for the expected secondary adrenal insufficiency, with gradual withdrawal
Monitor growth and height velocity and support catch-up growth, with growth hormone therapy and pubertal induction where needed
Manage hypertension, glucose intolerance and reduced bone density
Long-term surveillance for persistent or recurrent hypercortisolism
Coordinate care through paediatric endocrinology and a pituitary multidisciplinary team
